what_it_does: Serverless computing relies on spinning up fresh copies of a program almost instantly in response to incoming requests. The standard UNIX way to duplicate a running process — called fork() — works well on a single machine but is painfully slow across a network because it requires serializing and copying the entire program's memory over the wire. CXL (Compute Express Link) is a relatively new hardware standard that lets multiple servers share a pool of memory chips as if they were local, connected via a very fast link. CXLfork exploits this shared memory pool to clone a process onto a remote server without copying anything over the network: the remote server simply starts using the same memory pages already resident in the shared pool. Hot (frequently accessed) pages stay in the server's own fast local memory; cooler pages live in the shared CXL pool. This makes serverless cold-start latency — the delay before the first request is handled — dramatically shorter.
